claim: Drosophila suzukii invaded California in 2008.
source: Drosophila suzukii, endemic to Southeast Asia, invaded California in 2008 (Hauser, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hauser, 2011.

claim: D. suzukii has now emerged in Northern Europe.
source: It moved rapidly across the United States and has now emerged in Northern Europe as well (Asplen et al., 2015; Cini et al., 2012; Deprá et al., 2014; Dos Santos et al., 2017; Walsh et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: D. suzukii is a threat to a wide variety of fruit crops, including strawberries, blueberries, peaches, cherries, and grapes.
source: D. suzukii is a threat to a wide variety of fruit crops, including strawberries, blueberries, peaches, cherries, and grapes (Burrack et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2011; Mazzi et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: D. melanogaster lays eggs in fermenting fruit that is of no commercial value.
source: Whereas related species such as Drosophila melanogaster lay eggs in fermenting fruit that is of no commercial value, D. suzukii lays eggs in ripe fruit, leading to larval infestations and microbial infections that destroy crops (Karageorgi et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2011; Walsh et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations and contrasts with D. suzukii behavior.

claim: D. suzukii lays eggs in ripe fruit, leading to larval infestations and microbial infections that destroy crops.
source: Whereas related species such as Drosophila melanogaster lay eggs in fermenting fruit that is of no commercial value, D. suzukii lays eggs in ripe fruit, leading to larval infestations and microbial infections that destroy crops (Karageorgi et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2011; Walsh et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The adaptation of D. suzukii to ripe fruits has been accompanied by the evolution of a large serrated ovipositor, which penetrates the surface of ripe fruit and deposits an egg.
source: The adaptation of D. suzukii to ripe fruits has been accompanied by the evolution of a large serrated ovipositor, which penetrates the surface of ripe fruit and deposits an egg (Atallah et al., 2014; Green et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on ovipositor evolution.

claim: Changes in the olfactory and mechanosensory systems contribute to the adaptation of D. suzukii to its new niche.
source: A recent study showed that changes in the olfactory and mechanosensory systems contribute to the adaptation of D. suzukii to its new niche (Karageorgi et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Karageorgi et al., 2017.

claim: D. melanogaster laid the most eggs on the purée of the fermented stage of strawberry (Stage 7).
source: Whereas D. melanogaster laid the most eggs on the purée of the fermented stage of strawberry (Stage 7, Figure 1C), D. suzukii females laid the fewest eggs on this fermented stage (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: D. suzukii females laid the fewest eggs on the fermented stage of strawberry.
source: Whereas D. melanogaster laid the most eggs on the purée of the fermented stage of strawberry (Stage 7, Figure 1C), D. suzukii females laid the fewest eggs on this fermented stage (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: D. suzukii laid more eggs on the white-green and ripe stages (Stages 1 and 5) of strawberry.
source: Rather, D. suzukii laid more eggs on the white-green and ripe stages (Stages 1 and 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the oviposition assay described in the text and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: D. biarmipes did not show strong oviposition preferences among different strawberry ripening stages.
source: We also tested a third species, D. biarmipes, which is phylogenetically much closer to D. suzukii than to D. melanogaster (Figure 1A), and did not find strong preferences (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: D. biarmipes laid a smaller number of eggs than D. melanogaster and D. suzukii in the multiple-choice oviposition experiment.
source: We note that this species laid a smaller number of eggs than the other two species in this experiment.
evidence: The claim is based on observation from the experiment described in the text.

claim: D. melanogaster preferred overripe fruit in a two-choice assay between ripe and overripe strawberry.
source: D. melanogaster preferred the overripe fruit, whereas D. suzukii preferred the ripe fruit, as expected (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: D. suzukii preferred ripe fruit in a two-choice assay between ripe and overripe strawberry.
source: D. melanogaster preferred the overripe fruit, whereas D. suzukii preferred the ripe fruit, as expected (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Gr33a is a receptor that is expressed in many taste neurons and is required for behavioral and physiological responses to many bitter tastants.
source: We then tested D. melanogaster mutant for Gr33a (gustatory receptor), a receptor that is expressed in many taste neurons and is required for behavioral and physiological responses to many bitter tastants (Dweck and Carlson, 2020; Moon et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Gr33a2 mutant showed a shift in oviposition preference similar to that of D. suzukii.
source: Surprisingly, Gr33a2 showed a shift in preference similar to that of D. suzukii (Figure 2C; the genetic background control is w1118 Canton-S, p<0.0001, n = 18, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C with statistical analysis.

claim: Gr33a3 mutant showed a shift in oviposition preference similar to that of D. suzukii.
source: We confirmed this shift with another allele, Gr33a3, and a different source of strawberries (Figure 2D, p<0.01, n = 19–20).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D with statistical analysis.

claim: D. suzukii has lost 20% of the bitter-sensing sensilla from the labellum.
source: D. suzukii has lost 20% of the bitter-sensing sensilla from the labellum, the major taste organ of the head.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by anatomical data presented in the Results section.

claim: D. suzukii has fewer labellar sensilla than D. melanogaster.
source: D. suzukii has fewer labellar sensilla. On each half-labellum of D. suzukii and D. biarmipes there are 27, rather than 31, sensilla as in D. melanogaster.
evidence: The claim is supported by anatomical data from scanning electron microscopy.

claim: The numbers of S sensilla and I sensilla are each reduced by two in D. suzukii compared to D. melanogaster.
source: The numbers of S sensilla and I sensilla are each reduced by two (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Sensilla in D. suzukii are much longer than in D. melanogaster.
source: A striking difference in sensillum morphology was found between D. suzukii and D. melanogaster: sensilla in D. suzukii are much longer.
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological measurements from scanning electron microscopy.

claim: S sensilla of D. suzukii are ~43–53 μm long compared to ~20–30 μm in D. melanogaster.
source: S sensilla of D. suzukii are ~43–53 μm long compared to ~20–30 μm in D. melanogaster; I sensilla are ~57–63 μm vs. 30–40 μm; L sensilla are ~73–100 μm vs. ~ 40–50 μm.
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological measurements.

claim: L sensilla of D. suzukii showed little or no response to any tested bitter compound.
source: We found that L sensilla of D. suzukii showed little or no response to any tested bitter compound (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Two S sensilla, S3 and S7, showed little response to bitter compounds in D. suzukii.
source: Two S sensilla, S3 and S7, also showed little response to bitter compounds (n < 10 spikes/s to all tastants).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data.

claim: The strongest responses in D. suzukii were from several S sensilla to escin (ESC) and aristolochic acid (ARI), ~60 spikes/s in each case.
source: The strongest responses were from several S sensilla to escin (ESC) and aristolochic acid (ARI), ~60 spikes/s in each case (Figures 4 and 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figures 4 and 5A.

claim: DEET and saponin (SAP) elicited little or no response from any sensillum in D. suzukii.
source: Some bitter compounds, such as DEET and saponin (SAP), elicited little or no response from any sensillum.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data.

claim: D. melanogaster differs markedly from D. suzukii and D. biarmipes in its strong responses of I sensilla to CAF, UMB, and TPH.
source: D. melanogaster differs markedly from the other two species in its strong responses of I sensilla, that is, the responses of I8, I9, and I10 to CAF, UMB, and TPH. These responses are virtually absent in D. suzukii and D. biarmipes, even at higher concentrations (Figures 4 and 5A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in multiple figures.

claim: D. suzukii differs from both D. melanogaster and D. biarmipes in having little or no response to DEET or SAP.
source: D. suzukii differs from both D. melanogaster and D. biarmipes in having little or no response to DEET or SAP (Figures 4 and 5C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figures 4 and 5C,D.

claim: D. suzukii has evolved stronger responses to ARI than are observed in either D. melanogaster or D. biarmipes.
source: By contrast, D. suzukii has evolved stronger responses to ARI than are observed in either of the other species (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Labellar sensilla of D. suzukii fell into four functional classes based on hierarchical cluster analysis.
source: To determine the number of functional classes of sensilla on the labellum of D. suzukii, we performed a hierarchical cluster analysis. Sensilla fell into four functional classes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by cluster analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The response of S sensilla to ripe strawberry was low in all three species.
source: The response of S sensilla to ripe strawberry was low in all three species (Figure 6A, left).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Total spike input to ripe strawberry was lower in D. suzukii and D. biarmipes than in D. melanogaster in both S-a and S-b sensilla.
source: However, total spike input was lower in D. suzukii and D. biarmipes than in D. melanogaster in both S-a and S-b (Figure 6B, left; p<0.05, one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's multiple comparison test, n = 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6B with statistical analysis.

claim: All S sensilla of D. melanogaster responded to overripe strawberry.
source: Whereas all S sensilla of D. melanogaster responded, there was little or no response of any S-a or S-b sensilla of D. suzukii.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data.

claim: There was little or no response of any S-a or S-b sensilla of D. suzukii to overripe strawberry.
source: Whereas all S sensilla of D. melanogaster responded, there was little or no response of any S-a or S-b sensilla of D. suzukii.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data.

claim: The response of S sensilla to overripe strawberry was eliminated or severely reduced in Gr33a mutants.
source: We found that the response was eliminated or severely reduced, in each of three S sensilla tested: S5, which is an S-b sensillum, and S6 and S7, which are of the S-a class (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: D. suzukii shows a striking loss of response to certain bitter compounds in tarsal sensilla.
source: D. suzukii shows a striking loss of response to certain bitter compounds.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data from tarsal recordings.

claim: Coumarin (COU) and DEET both elicit excitatory responses from f5b, f4s, and f4c in both D. melanogaster and D. biarmipes, but few, if any, excitatory responses from any sensilla in D. suzukii.
source: Coumarin (COU) and DEET both elicit excitatory responses from f5b, f4s, and f4c in both D. melanogaster and D. biarmipes, but few, if any, excitatory responses (n > 0 spikes/s) from any sensilla in D. suzukii; interestingly, both tastants appear to inhibit f5s (Figure 7A,C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 7A,C,D.

claim: D. melanogaster avoided laying eggs on COU, lobeline hydrochloride (LOB), DEET, and denatonium benzoate (DEN) at 0.5 mM concentrations.
source: D. melanogaster avoided laying eggs on COU, lobeline hydrochloride (LOB), DEET, and denatonium benzoate (DEN), and D. biarmipes avoided COU, LOB, DEN, and sparteine sulfate salt (SPS).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data from two-choice oviposition assays.

claim: D. biarmipes avoided laying eggs on COU, LOB, DEN, and sparteine sulfate salt (SPS) at 0.5 mM concentrations.
source: D. melanogaster avoided laying eggs on COU, lobeline hydrochloride (LOB), DEET, and denatonium benzoate (DEN), and D. biarmipes avoided COU, LOB, DEN, and sparteine sulfate salt (SPS).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data from two-choice oviposition assays.

claim: D. suzukii oviposition was not deterred by any of the tested bitter compounds at 0.5 mM concentrations.
source: Remarkably, D. suzukii oviposition was not deterred by any of these bitter compounds (Figure 8B).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: D. suzukii showed no oviposition deterrence at higher concentrations of DEET, SPS, COU, LOB, and DEN.
source: D. suzukii again showed no deterrence at either of the higher concentrations of any tested compound (Figure 8C; one-way ANOVA followed by Dunnett's multiple comparison test, p>0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 8C with statistical analysis.

claim: The labellar transcription profile of D. suzukii is more closely related to that of D. biarmipes than that of D. melanogaster.
source: The labellar transcription profile of D. suzukii is more closely related to that of D. biarmipes than that of D. melanogaster, as determined by a hierarchical cluster analysis (Figure 9A).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptomic analysis shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Seven Gr genes are expressed at levels fourfold lower or less in D. suzukii than in D. melanogaster.
source: Of 38 Grs whose expression was detected in this study, seven are expressed at levels fourfold lower or less in D. suzukii than in D. melanogaster (Figure 9C, log2FC<-2, adjusted p-value<0.01, Supplementary files 1–4).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptomic data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Five Gr genes expressed in bitter-sensing neurons (Gr8a, Gr22e, Gr22f, Gr32a, and Gr98d) are expressed at levels fourfold lower or less in D. suzukii than in D. melanogaster.
source: Interestingly, five of these, Gr8a, Gr22e, Gr22f, Gr32a, and Gr98d, have been found previously to be expressed in bitter-sensing neurons (Weiss et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptomic data and citations to previous studies.

claim: Gr22f expression was undetectable in D. suzukii by RNAseq.
source: Gr22f is a particularly striking case. Its expression was detected in both D. melanogaster and D. biarmipes, but was undetectable in D. suzukii by RNAseq even with 50 million paired-reads for a sample.
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptomic data.

claim: Gr22f product was amplified by RT-PCR from D. melanogaster and D. biarmipes labellar RNA, but little, if any, product was observed from a D. suzukii preparation.
source: Consistent with the RNAseq results, a Gr22f product was amplified by RT-PCR from D. melanogaster and D. biarmipes labellar RNA, but little, if any, product was observed from a D. suzukii preparation (Figure 9—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Mutation of Gr22f in D. melanogaster reduces the response to DEN in the S-b sensilla.
source: Interestingly, mutation of Gr22f in D. melanogaster reduces the response to DEN in the S-b sensilla (Sung et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sung et al., 2017.

claim: IR21a was expressed more abundantly than any other IR in D. suzukii, including the co-receptor genes.
source: Curiously, in all three replicates of the D. suzukii labellar transcriptome, IR21a was expressed more abundantly than any other IR, including the co-receptor genes.
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptomic data.

claim: IR21a was expressed ~85 times more abundantly in D. suzukii than in D. melanogaster.
source: IR21a was expressed ~85 times more abundantly in D. suzukii than in D. melanogaster.
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptomic data.

claim: Cyp6g1 is more abundant in D. suzukii than in D. melanogaster (100-fold) and D. biarmipes (5-fold).
source: We note finally an observation that may have significance for pest control: Cyp6g1 and Cyp12d1-p are more abundant in D. suzukii than in D. melanogaster (100- and 25-fold, respectively) and D. biarmipes (5- and 20-fold, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptomic data.

claim: Cyp12d1-p is more abundant in D. suzukii than in D. melanogaster (25-fold) and D. biarmipes (20-fold).
source: We note finally an observation that may have significance for pest control: Cyp6g1 and Cyp12d1-p are more abundant in D. suzukii than in D. melanogaster (100- and 25-fold, respectively) and D. biarmipes (5- and 20-fold, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptomic data.

claim: Overexpression of Cyp6g1 in D. melanogaster increases resistance to insecticides, including DDT.
source: Overexpression of either gene in D. melanogaster increases resistance to insecticides, including Dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane (DDT) (Daborn et al., 2007; Festucci-Buselli et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Overexpression of Cyp12d1-p in D. melanogaster increases resistance to insecticides, including DDT.
source: Overexpression of either gene in D. melanogaster increases resistance to insecticides, including Dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane (DDT) (Daborn et al., 2007; Festucci-Buselli et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Plants produce a vast diversity of toxins to defend themselves against insect attack.
source: Plants produce a vast diversity of toxins to defend themselves against insect attack (Biere et al., 2004; Frost et al., 2008; Fürstenberg-Hägg et al., 2013; Ibanez et al., 2012; War et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Many plant toxins are secondary metabolites that taste bitter to humans.
source: Many of these compounds are secondary metabolites that taste bitter to humans (Dagan-Wiener et al., 2017; Drewnowski and Gomez-Carneros, 2000; Keast et al., 2003; Wiener et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Insects have evolved mechanisms for detecting bitter compounds and avoiding them; these compounds thus deter feeding and oviposition.
source: Insects in turn have evolved mechanisms for detecting these bitter compounds and avoiding them; these compounds thus deter feeding and oviposition (Briscoe et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2019; Pontes et al., 2014; Salloum et al., 2011; Sellier et al., 2011; Wada-Katsumata et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Levels of bitter compounds differ among various stages of fruit ripening.
source: Since levels of bitter compounds differ among various stages of fruit ripening, it seems plausible that the sensitivity of an insect to different bitter compounds may influence its choice of a ripening stage on which to lay eggs (Batista-Silva et al., 2018; Cheng and Breen, 1991; Taghadomi-Saberi et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on fruit ripening.

claim: Bitter-sensing neurons are housed in taste sensilla in the labellum, the tarsal segments of the legs, and the pharynx in D. melanogaster.
source: Bitter-sensing neurons are housed in taste sensilla in the labellum (one of the mouthparts), the tarsal segments of the legs, and the pharynx (Chen and Dahanukar, 2017; Delventhal and Carlson, 2016; Dweck and Carlson, 2020; Lee et al., 2010; Lee et al., 2015; Ling et al., 2014; Marella et al., 2006; Meunier et al., 2003; Moon et al., 2009; Poudel and Lee, 2016; Rimal et al., 2020; Sang et al., 2019; Weiss et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Bitter responses depend largely on the Gr (gustatory receptor) family.
source: Although there are several kinds of taste receptors, bitter responses depend largely on the Gr (gustatory receptor) family (Clyne et al., 2000; Joseph and Carlson, 2015; Liman et al., 2014; Scott, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Many Gr genes have been found to be required for response to individual bitter compounds.
source: Many Gr genes have been found to be required for response to individual bitter compounds (Dweck and Carlson, 2020; Lee et al., 2010; Lee et al., 2015; Moon et al., 2009; Poudel and Lee, 2016; Rimal et al., 2020; Sang et al., 2019; Weiss et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Expression of certain Gr genes in sugar-sensing neurons confers response to bitter compounds.
source: Moreover, expression of certain Gr genes in sugar-sensing neurons confers response to bitter compounds (Dweck and Carlson, 2020; Shim et al., 2015; Sung et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: D. biarmipes is phylogenetically much closer to D. suzukii than to D. melanogaster.
source: We also tested a third species, D. biarmipes, which is phylogenetically much closer to D. suzukii than to D. melanogaster (Figure 1A), and did not find strong preferences (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by the phylogenetic tree shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Levels of flavonoids decline as a function of developmental stage in strawberries.
source: For example, levels of flavonoids, many of which taste bitter to humans, decline as a function of developmental stage in strawberries (Cheng and Breen, 1991).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cheng and Breen, 1991.

claim: D. sechellia has specialized on the noni fruit (Morinda citrifolia), which is toxic to other species.
source: For example, Drosophila sechellia has specialized on the noni fruit (Morinda citrifolia), which is toxic to other species, and Drosophila erecta has specialized on screw pine fruit (Pandanus spp.) (Jones, 1998; Linz et al., 2013; Whiteman and Pierce, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: D. erecta has specialized on screw pine fruit (Pandanus spp.).
source: For example, Drosophila sechellia has specialized on the noni fruit (Morinda citrifolia), which is toxic to other species, and Drosophila erecta has specialized on screw pine fruit (Pandanus spp.) (Jones, 1998; Linz et al., 2013; Whiteman and Pierce, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: D. sechellia and D. erecta have retained the canonical numbers and map positions of taste sensilla defined originally in D. melanogaster.
source: D. suzukii differs from D. sechellia and D. erecta in that it has lost taste sensilla from the labellum; D. sechellia and D. erecta have retained the canonical numbers and map positions of taste sensilla defined originally in D. melanogaster (Dweck and Carlson, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dweck and Carlson, 2020.

claim: Analysis of the D. sechellia genome suggested that the rapid loss of 12 bitter Grs contributed to a loss of taste responses to bitter secondary metabolites of noni fruit.
source: First, analysis of the D. sechellia genome suggested that the rapid loss of 12 bitter Grs contributed to a loss of taste responses to bitter secondary metabolites of noni fruit (McBride, 2007; McBride et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to McBride, 2007 and McBride et al., 2007.

claim: Oviposition preference in D. sechellia was found to depend on two genes expressed in the legs, Obp57d and Obp57e.
source: Second, oviposition preference in D. sechellia was found to depend on two genes expressed in the legs, Obp57d (odorant binding protein) and Obp57e, leading to the suggestion that an evolutionary change in tarsal taste response contributed to its shift in oviposition preference (Matsuo et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Matsuo et al., 2007.

claim: IR21a has been implicated in cool sensing.
source: IR21a has been implicated in cool sensing, raising interesting questions about the regulation and function of this receptor (Ni et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ni et al., 2016.

claim: 162 genes were differentially expressed between D. suzukii and both D. melanogaster and D. biarmipes.
source: We found 162 genes differentially expressed between D. suzukii and both of the other two species, as determined by the following conservative statistical criteria: |log2 Fold Change| > 2, and adjusted p-value<0.01 across all of four different differential expression (DE) analysis pipelines (Supplementary file 3, Supplementary file 4; see Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptomic analysis with statistical criteria.

claim: Of the 162 differentially expressed genes, 13% were associated with the GO term 'sensory perception of chemical stimulus,' a fivefold enrichment compared to the set of all genes expressed in the labellum of any species.
source: Of these 162 genes, 13% were associated with the GO term 'sensory perception of chemical stimulus,' a fivefold enrichment compared to the set of all genes expressed in the labellum of any species (adjusted p-value=2.99E-5).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology analysis with statistical significance.

claim: The saw-like ovipositor of D. suzukii facilitates egg laying in ripening fruit that other drosophilid species cannot use.
source: The saw-like ovipositor of D. suzukii is larger and facilitates egg laying in ripening fruit that other drosophilid species cannot use (Atallah et al., 2014; Harris et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The ovipositor of D. suzukii does not have structures with pores at their tips, suggesting they do not function in taste.
source: We did not observe a pore at the tip of any of these structures, suggesting that they do not function in taste.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the absence of pores, which are characteristic of taste sensilla.

claim: The loss of bitter response in D. suzukii contributes to its novel oviposition preference for ripe fruit.
source: These findings support a model in which bitter compounds in early ripening stages deter egg laying in most Drosophila species, but a loss of bitter response contributes to the adaptation of D. suzukii to ripe fruit.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple lines of evidence presented in the study.

claim: Bitter compounds in early ripening stages deter egg laying in most Drosophila species.
source: These findings support a model in which bitter compounds in early ripening stages deter egg laying in most Drosophila species, but a loss of bitter response contributes to the adaptation of D. suzukii to ripe fruit.
evidence: The claim is part of a model inferred from the data presented in the study.

claim: Changes in bitter taste perception have accompanied the adaptation of D. suzukii to ripe fruit.
source: We found that changes in bitter taste perception have accompanied this adaptation.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by multiple lines of evidence in the Results section.

claim: Physiological responses to various bitter compounds are lost in D. suzukii.
source: Physiological responses to various bitter compounds are lost.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by electrophysiological data in the Results section.

claim: Responses to strawberry purées are lost from two classes of taste sensilla in D. suzukii.
source: Responses to strawberry purées are lost from two classes of taste sensilla.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by electrophysiological data in the Results section.

claim: Egg laying in D. suzukii is not deterred by bitter compounds that deter other species.
source: Egg laying is not deterred by bitter compounds that deter other species.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by behavioral data in the Results section.

claim: Profiling of labellar transcriptomes reveals reduced expression of several bitter Gr genes in D. suzukii.
source: Profiling of labellar transcriptomes reveals reduced expression of several bitter Gr genes (gustatory receptors).
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by transcriptomic data in the Results section.
